name: Factory Method
intent: Let subclasses decide which concrete object to create, while shared code works with the abstract type.
scenario: A delivery app plans shipments. Road delivery uses trucks, sea delivery uses ships. The planning code should not care which.
problem: Your planning code needs a transport object, but which one depends on the kind of delivery. Writing new Truck() or new Ship() inside the planner ties it to every concrete class, and every new vehicle means editing it.
solution: Move creation into one overridable method, the factory method. The base class calls createTransport() inside its planning logic. Each subclass overrides it to return its own product. The planner only ever sees the Transport interface.
pain: planDelivery() contains an if/else that knows Truck and Ship
Adding air delivery means editing that function (and every copy of the switch)
The planner cannot be tested without real transports
Choosing the transport and using it are tangled together
benefits: planDelivery() only knows the Transport interface
Air delivery is a new subclass, with no edits to existing code
Tests can subclass and return a fake transport
whenToUse: A class cannot know in advance which concrete type it will need
You want subclasses or configuration to choose the type, not the caller
You want a clear extension point for adding new product types
whenNotToUse: There is only one product type and no sign of more: just use new
A plain function that returns the right object is enough (a simple factory function)
Adding a subclass per variant is heavier than the problem deserves
pitfalls: Subclass explosion: one creator class per product can pile up quickly
People call this pattern Simple Factory or static factory; those are different and simpler
The base class method name must be documented as an extension point, or nobody knows to override it
Returning an unrelated type breaks the contract the planner relies on
